blocks.text: Feed Charge Pump PU-2101B — Mechanical Seal Leakage
Isolate PU-2101B, swap to spare PU-2101A, replace mechanical seal cartridge
Mechanical seal of Feed Charge Pump PU-2101B failed on 12-Mar-2026, causing seal leakage and an unplanned feed reduction to the ARP reactor section.
ARP produced resin grade PR-5502 (Reactor Rate ± 13.6 T/H). Field operator noted minor seal weep on PU-2101B during routine round.
Seal flush low-flow alarm annunciated; visible feed seal leak with low suction pressure. Pump auto-tripped on low discharge pressure.
Feed section reduced; charge to reactor curtailed pending seal repair. Rotating team mobilized.
Seal cartridge & shaft sleeve inspected — seal faces heat-checked / worn (dry-running signature).
New seal cartridge installed, pump commissioned, feed restored to ± 13.6 T/H.
Problem: Mechanical seal of Feed Charge Pump PU-2101B failed on 12-Mar-2026, causing seal leakage and an unplanned feed reduction to the ARP reactor section.

PU-2101B seal MTBF trended down from 26 to 9 months over the last 3 cycles. Seal-flush flow had been intermittently below the 6 L/min design minimum during feed swings, indicating recurring dry-run exposure.
Mechanical seal of PU-2101B leaked / failed
Reduced charge feed to ARP reactor section

Suction pressure dropped during feed swing; NPSH margin < 0.5 m (spec ≥ 1.0 m) — cavitation risk.

Cooling water to seal cooler inadequate
Seal cooler outlet temp normal (42 °C) — cooling adequate.
Seal in service 11 months, within 24-month design life.

Seal-flush plan (Plan 11) not on the PM check-sheet.
Operators trained; no competency gap identified.

CASE 1
Topic
This case focuses on reducing  improper execution risk caused by 
scattered knowledge source, missing tacit knowledge, difficulty in 
finding trusted information, and disconnected operational data. 
Background
In a chemical manufacturing plant, engineers need to make quick and 
accurate decisions during start
 -
up, troubleshooting, maintenance 
activities, and abnormal operating conditions. However, the 
information they need is often spread across different sources: SOPs 
are stored in one system, datasheets in another, P&IDs in document 
folders, maintenance logs in separate records, and real
 -
time operating 
data in plant systems.
Because these knowledge sources are not connected, engineers may 
spend too much time searching for trusted information or asking 
experienced personnel for confirmation. In some cases, missing tacit 
knowledge, outdated documents, or incomplete context may cause 
teams to misinterpret procedures or fail to follow the correct execution 
steps. 
As a result, plant operations may face longer troubleshooting time, 
repeated engineering rework, higher safety risk, delayed start
 -
up, and 
inconsistent decision
 -
making across Process, Maintenance, 
Engineering, Operation, and HSE functions.

Participants are challenged to design an AI
 -
enabled Manufacturing 
Knowledge Hub that scattered plant knowledge from SOPs, 
datasheets, P&IDs, EDMS, AIMS, maintenance logs, incident reports, 
and real
 -
time operational data into one trusted, structured, and 
traceable knowledge ecosystem. The solution should help engineers 
find verified information faster, reduce improper execution, support 
troubleshooting, and improve reliability, safety, and cross
 -
functional 
decision
 -
making.

language questions and context

based search.

generated answers with

confidence indicators.

hub with EDMS, AIMS, and Digital Twin to provide technical
